newsitem.title: DUBAI: FEATURE - Money and adventure lure Western nurses to Saudi.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Money and adventure lure Western nurses to Saudi.

text.p: Promises of money and the lure of adventure have led thousands of Western nurses to leave their homes and work in the conservative kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

From Europe, Australia and North America, female nurses flock to the oil-rich desert state where income is tax-free and hospitals provide furnished accommodation with swimming pools and tennis courts.

Despite Saudi Arabia's strict Islamic laws -- which forbid women to drive and require them to wear long black robes in public -- many nurses say they enjoy the work and look forward to the sizzling Arabian nights.
"What attracted me was that I could earn the salary without paying tax and had the potential to save and travel," said a Canadian nurse who worked in the capital Riyadh for four years.
"The only thing we had to pay for in terms of basics was food and long-distance phone calls."
MURDER FOCUSES ATTENTION ON FOREIGN NURSES

International attention focused on the situation of foreign nurses in Saudi Arabia when two British nurses were arrested on charges of murdering an Australian colleague in December at the hospital complex in eastern Saudi Arabia where they worked.

Yvonne Gilford was found stabbed 13 times, bludgeoned and suffocated in her room at the King Fahd military medical complex in Dhahran on December 11, just days before her 56th birthday. She had been in the kingdom for about six months.
The same month Deborah Parry, 38, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31, were charged with her murder.
A verdict in the case is expected in the next few days. If found guilty, the defendants could face execution by sword under Saudi Arabia's Islamic sharia law.
Medical sources say Saudi Arabia has some of the best hospitals in the region, but relies heavily on foreigners to staff them.
The state's five-year plan to 2000 identifies only 11.2 percent of the 57,000 nurses in the kingdom as Saudi nationals.

Embassies said about 2,000 U.S. nurses and almost 1,000 British nurses work in Riyadh alone. Some 2,000 Australian nurses are scattered across the country, along with colleagues from Canada, Ireland and other European states.
Nurses are also recruited from the Indian subcontinent and southeast Asia.
Some 300 hospitals have been built in the kingdom, and many have sprawling housing units, recreation facilities and shops.
"Some of the compounds are huge with cinemas, gyms and swimming pools," said one former hospital employee. "You don't feel like you are in Saudi Arabia."
COMPOUNDS ALLOW FREEDOM BUT ARE CONFINING

The kingdom's conservative Islamic society makes it all but impossible for women to live on their own outside a housing complex. Most foreigners who work in there chose to live in compounds, where most Saudi restrictions fall away.
At the same time, residents say the compounds confine them to live, work and socialise with the same people, in the same space, every day.

The compounds are like self-contained villages, surrounded by walls. Step inside and you are in another world where women wear shorts and put on the mandatory black "abaya" robes only when they venture beyond the walls.
Even at work, nurses are exempt from the Islamic dress code.
Western diplomats said nurses from their countries earn 8,000 to 12,000 riyals ($2,100-$3,200) a month, depending on nationality, with U.S. staff in the highest salary bracket.
"You don't always have a higher salary than you did at home, but now it's tax-free and you've got no bills, no rent, no car insurance, of course, because you can't drive," the nurse said.
After a hard week at work, nurses are known to party hard.
"There were some rip-roaring parties and you drank and danced and partied," one nurse said.
"Some got way out of control. People would jump off rooftops into pools and clothes would come off. But people try to be careful because they know they could go to jail."
The Canadian nurse said some colleagues became depressed in Saudi Arabia and could not cope with life there.
But tragedies on the compounds are rare, nurses said.
"In the four years I was there we had two suicides and one woman went strange and ended up threatening to get a gun to kill herself...," the Canadian nurse said.
Nurses described some of their colleagues who came to work in Saudi Arabia as misfits who could not handle life at home.
"Going to Saudi Arabia is sort of an escape. It's easy there in a way because everything is structured in the compound. You escape the pressures of normal society," a British nurse said.
